slides.title: Finite integer domains make boundaries unavoidable
keyPoints: An unsigned width has a finite maximum
Application limits may be smaller than type limits
Arithmetic rules depend on operand types
slides.narration: An integer type is not the unbounded set of whole numbers from mathematics. An unsigned type with w value bits represents zero through two to the w minus one. That finite domain matters when a program counts bytes or combines input dimensions. The application may impose a smaller limit, such as a maximum packet size, even when the type could represent a much larger value. Begin by separating mathematical intent, the expression's actual type, and the final allowed domain. A value can fit the machine type and still violate policy. It can also wrap under defined unsigned arithmetic and stop representing the mathematical quantity you intended.
actions: Choose a small application limit and distinguish it from the integer type’s maximum.

question.prompt: Does a representable allocation size automatically meet the application’s resource policy?
question.answer: No. A type limit and an application limit are different constraints. Both may need checking.

slides.title: The most negative value has no matching positive partner
keyPoints: Two’s complement has an asymmetric range
The high bit has a negative positional weight
Negating the minimum needs a separate case
slides.narration: In an eight-bit two's-complement model, values run from negative one hundred twenty-eight through positive one hundred twenty-seven. There is one extra negative value because zero occupies one of the nonnegative patterns. The high bit is not a separate minus sign: it contributes negative one hundred twenty-eight. Thus 10000101 means negative one hundred twenty-three, not negative five. This asymmetry explains why negating the minimum signed value cannot produce a representable result in the same type. A machine may produce some bit pattern, but ordinary overflowing signed C++ arithmetic is not justified by that observation. Check the boundary before computing an absolute value or a negation.
actions: Decode 10000101 using positional weights and compare it with negative five.

question.prompt: Why is flipping only the high bit not a general two’s-complement negation?
question.answer: The high bit is a negative weight, not a sign-magnitude flag. Negation changes the complete representation, and the minimum needs special treatment.

slides.title: Reject signed overflow before evaluating the operation
keyPoints: An optional result distinguishes rejection
The guard precedes signed addition
Unsigned wrap follows a different rule
slides.narration: increment accepts seven and returns an optional containing eight. At the largest int, it returns no value before evaluating value plus one, so no signed overflow occurs. The second line reports maximum rejected=true. The final expression deliberately uses unsigned arithmetic: its maximum plus one wraps to zero under the language's modular rule. That zero is defined, but whether wrap is useful depends on the requirement. An optional makes rejection visible without choosing a valid integer as a special error sentinel. The program does not infer the size of int or print a platform-specific maximum. It tests the required relationship at whatever supported width the implementation provides.
actions: Predict the three lines and separate signed rejection from unsigned modular behavior.

slides.title: A wrapped size can look reassuringly small
keyPoints: This is a labeled eight-bit arithmetic model
Seventeen elements of width sixteen need 272 bytes
Checking the reduced value accepts the wrong quantity
slides.narration: The real unsigned multiplication here safely computes two hundred seventy-two. We then explicitly mask to eight bits to model a narrow byte-count calculation, obtaining sixteen. The modeled narrow check accepts sixteen under a sixty-four-byte policy limit and prints true. The exact required size is still two hundred seventy-two. The final division-based check rejects the request and prints false, without multiplying an untrusted large pair. This program does not allocate a too-small buffer or perform an out-of-bounds write. It isolates how a bad arithmetic representation can make later bounds checking approve the wrong quantity. In real allocation code, that mistake can invalidate every later access assumption.

keyPoints: Checking count * width only after multiplication may observe a wrapped unsigned result. Signed overflow is undefined behavior.
A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Multiply first and compare the result with limit. An unsigned wrapped result can be small enough to pass.

The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: When width is nonzero, require count <= limit/width before forming the product. Use a separate state to represent rejection.

slides.title: Unsigned Integers
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: An unsigned w -bit value interprets every bit as a nonnegative positional weight.
The value is the sum of b_i * 2^i over positions 0 through w-1 .
There is no sign bit in this interpretation.
Every pattern represents a value.
slides.narration: An unsigned w -bit value interprets every bit as a nonnegative positional weight. The value is the sum of b_i * 2^i over positions 0 through w-1 . There is no sign bit in this interpretation. Every pattern represents a value. For eight bits, 11111111 is 128+64+32+16+8+4+2+1 = 255 . This direct relationship makes unsigned types useful for masks, counters with explicitly modular behavior, and binary fields. It does not make unsigned the best choice for every ordinary quantity, especially where negative error indicators or differences are meaningful. The minimum unsigned value is zero. The maximum is 2^w - 1 , because the sum of all positional weights below 2^w is one less than 2^w . An eight-bit unsigned type spans 0 through 255; a 16-bit type spans 0 through 65,535. The number of values is one greater than the maximum because zero is included. This matters in capacity calculations and exhaustive tests. A field described as “eight bits” provides 256 distinct patterns, but a protocol may reserve some of them, reducing the set of valid application values. Unsigned arithmetic is performed modulo 2^w for the relevant unsigned type. Mathematically, values differing by a multiple of 2^w map to the same representation. In eight-bit arithmetic, 250 + 10 maps to 4 because 260 - 256 = 4 . Integer promotions can cause a small unsigned type’s expression to be evaluated in a wider signed type first. Assigning the result back to the narrow unsigned type still performs the specified conversion. State whether a trace is describing an eight-bit mathematical model or the exact promoted type of a C expression. The final stored pattern may agree even when the intermediate language operations differ.

An unsigned w -bit value interprets every bit as a nonnegative positional weight. The value is the sum of b_i * 2^i over positions 0 through w-1 . There is no sign bit in this interpretation. Every pattern represents a value. For eight bits, 11111111 is 128+64+32+16+8+4+2+1 = 255 . This direct relationship makes unsigned types useful for masks, counters with explicitly modular behavior, and binary fields. It does not make unsigned the best choice for every ordinary quantity, especially where negative error indicators or differences are meaningful. The minimum unsigned value is zero. The maximum is 2^w - 1 , because the sum of all positional weights below 2^w is one less than 2^w . An eight-bit unsigned type spans 0 through 255; a 16-bit type spans 0 through 65,535. The number of values is one greater than the maximum because zero is included. This matters in capacity calculations and exhaustive tests. A field described as “eight bits” provides 256 distinct patterns, but a protocol may reserve some of them, reducing the set of valid application values. Unsigned arithmetic is performed modulo 2^w for the relevant unsigned type. Mathematically, values differing by a multiple of 2^w map to the same representation. In eight-bit arithmetic, 250 + 10 maps to 4 because 260 - 256 = 4 . Integer promotions can cause a small unsigned type’s expression to be evaluated in a wider signed type first. Assigning the result back to the narrow unsigned type still performs the specified conversion. keyPoints: Two’s complement assigns the high bit a negative weight.
A w -bit pattern has value -b_(w-1)*2^(w-1) + sum(b_i*2^i) for the remaining positions.

slides.narration: Two’s complement assigns the high bit a negative weight. A w -bit pattern has value -b_(w-1)*2^(w-1) + sum(b_i*2^i) for the remaining positions. The range is -2^(w-1) through 2^(w-1)-1 . There is one more negative value than positive nonzero values. This is the representation used by the reference platform and required by C++20’s signed integer representation rules. C17 permits additional signed representations, so statements about their byte patterns must be treated as platform assumptions in a C17 program. Representation does not change the rule that overflowing ordinary signed arithmetic is undefined. In two’s complement, the most significant bit distinguishes nonnegative and negative values, but it is not an independent minus-sign flag. Flipping that bit alone does not generally negate the number. It changes the contribution of a power-of-two weight. For an eight-bit value, 00000101 is 5, while 10000101 is -128 + 5 = -123 , not -5. The representation of -5 is 11111011 . This is why sign-magnitude intuition gives incorrect results when interpreting ordinary machine integers. Nonnegative two’s-complement values have a zero high bit and the same low-bit encoding as their unsigned values. Eight-bit 37 is 00100101 . This shared encoding makes many machine operations work naturally for both signed and unsigned data, with the interpretation of flags or comparisons providing the difference. The largest positive eight-bit value is 01111111 , or 127. Incrementing it in a raw eight-bit hardware operation produces the pattern 10000000 . That observation does not license a C or C++ signed expression to overflow. The source-language contract and machine result must remain separate. A negative two’s-complement pattern can be interpreted by subtracting 2^w from its unsigned interpretation. For eight bits, 11110011 is 243 unsigned and 243 - 256 = -13 signed. This is often the quickest way to decode a negative pattern by hand. The minimum value has only the high bit set: 10000000 is -128. There is no positive 128 in the same signed type. This asymmetry is responsible for special cases in negation, absolute value, and division. Boundary tests should include the minimum, not merely small negative values. At the bit-pattern level, two’s-complement negation in a fixed width is obtained by inverting the bits and adding one, with the result reduced to that width. For eight-bit 13, 00001101 becomes 11110010 , then 11110011 , representing -13. The minimum value maps to its own pattern under this modular operation. In signed source arithmetic, negating the minimum is not representable and therefore is not a valid ordinary signed result. An absolute-value routine must check or use a representation that can hold the positive magnitude. Do not assume abs(x) is safe for every value of a signed type.

slides.narration: Conversion to an unsigned type produces the unique value congruent to the original integer modulo 2^w . Thus converting -1 to an eight-bit unsigned type yields 255, and converting -13 yields 243. This is a value-conversion rule, not merely a claim that implementations copy the same bytes. The conversion is useful when modular semantics are intended. It is dangerous when a negative length indicates an error. Check the signed value before converting it to size_t . Once -1 becomes a large positive size, later code can mistake the error for a huge valid allocation or copy request. When the value fits in the destination signed type, the value is preserved. For values outside the destination range, C17 and older C++ rules require special care: C17 permits an implementation-defined result or an implementation-defined signal. C++20 specifies the destination value congruent modulo 2^w , where w is the destination width. [ R8 , R35 ] Portable cross-language code should not depend on an unchecked out-of-range conversion. Validate against the destination’s maximum first when the semantic requirement is a nonnegative signed value. An explicit cast documents that a conversion occurs; it does not establish that losing range is acceptable. Widening a two’s-complement signed value preserves its value by repeating the sign bit in the newly added high positions. Eight-bit -13, 11110011 , becomes 16-bit 11111111 11110011 . Interpreting the widened pattern still gives -13. Sign extension is a representation consequence of value-preserving widening on this platform. A compiler may use a sign-extending instruction, fold the result into another operation, or already hold the value in a wider register. The required result matters more than the presence of one particular mnemonic. Widening an unsigned value preserves its value by filling new high positions with zeros. Eight-bit 243 becomes 00000000 11110011 in 16 bits. The low bits match the sign-extension example, but the high bits and interpreted value differ. When decoding a binary format, select extension based on the field’s declared meaning. A one-byte temperature offset may be signed; a one-byte payload length is normally unsigned. Narrowing to an unsigned type retains the low-order portion of the value modulo the destination range. For example, converting 0x1234 to an eight-bit unsigned value yields 0x34 . An encoder that silently narrows 300 to an eight-bit length can produce a header claiming 44 bytes while writing 300 bytes. Rejecting an out-of-range value preserves agreement between the representation and the data it describes.

slides.title: Integer Arithmetic
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Unsigned addition wraps according to its type.
Signed addition requires the mathematical result to be representable.
To check nonnegative unsigned addition before performing it, test b <= maximum - a .
For signed addition, use separate positive and negative cases or a documented checked-arithmetic facility.
slides.narration: Unsigned addition wraps according to its type. Signed addition requires the mathematical result to be representable. To check nonnegative unsigned addition before performing it, test b <= maximum - a . For signed addition, use separate positive and negative cases or a documented checked-arithmetic facility. Checking after a signed overflow is too late. An expression such as if (a + b < a) cannot reliably detect signed overflow because the addition itself may already violate the language’s requirements. Validate the operation’s precondition, not merely the resulting pattern. Unsigned subtraction also wraps. If an unsigned count is zero, subtracting one produces the maximum value, not -1. This is the classic failure in a reverse loop whose condition is i >= 0 : the condition is always true for an unsigned i . For lengths, subtraction is often safer than addition only after the order is established. To validate a region, first require offset <= total , then require length <= total - offset . This avoids overflow in offset + length while preventing unsigned underflow in the subtraction. Allocation and indexing frequently multiply a count by an element size. The product must fit before it is passed to an allocator. For nonzero s , require count <= SIZE_MAX / s . Then count * s is representable as size_t . A successful allocation of a wrapped, too-small product is more dangerous than a clean allocation failure. The code may later write the original number of elements into the undersized block. Treat multiplication validation as part of memory safety, not merely numerical correctness. Integer division discards a fractional part. For signed division in the language versions used here, truncation is toward zero: -7 / 3 is -2. The remainder satisfies a == (a/b)*b + a%b when the operations are defined, and its sign follows the dividend when nonzero. Division by zero is invalid. Dividing the minimum signed value by -1 is also invalid when the positive quotient cannot be represented. A checked division must handle both cases. Unsigned division does not have the signed-minimum case, but still requires a nonzero divisor. Overflow means the mathematical result exceeds the representable range. The consequence depends on the operation and type. Unsigned modular arithmetic is defined. Ordinary signed overflow is undefined. A machine instruction may set a carry or overflow flag, but an ordinary source expression does not automatically expose or check that flag. Use a tested checked-arithmetic routine when values approach limits. Compiler built-ins can help on supported compilers, but they are not part of the portable C17 or C++20 core interface. A library boundary should report range failure explicitly rather than returning a plausible wrapped size. For integers, “underflow” is often used informally for a result below the minimum representable value. Unsigned 0 - 1 wraps; signed subtraction below the minimum is undefined. Floating-point underflow has a different technical meaning involving tiny results, discussed in Chapter 5. Use precise language in diagnostics. “Negative length rejected” is more useful than “underflow happened” when the actual failure is invalid input. The distinction helps identify whether the fix belongs in input validation, type selection, or arithmetic checking. Wraparound is the cycling of a finite modular value through its range. It can be useful for checksums, sequence counters, and ring indices, but only when the algorithm is designed for it. Comparing modular sequence numbers requires a defined window of ambiguity; ordinary numeric order is not automatically the desired temporal order. For a ring of arbitrary capacity, index = (index + 1) % capacity is conceptually clear but still requires nonzero capacity and a representable increment. If the capacity is a power of two and the index domain is controlled, masking can implement the wrap. The optimization follows from the invariant; it does not replace it.

slides.narration: Suppose an input requests 1,500 records, each occupying 24 bytes, plus a 64-byte header. The required calculation is header + count*stride . The order of checks must prevent both multiplication and addition overflow. Companion listing: ch04/checked_size.cpp The multiplication produces 36,000. Adding 64 produces 36,064. The first guard ensures that the multiplication is valid in the size domain, while the second guard ensures that the header fits in the remaining range. A zero stride is allowed by this mathematical helper; an application can impose a stricter semantic rule before calling it. Now consider a count larger than maximum / 24 . The function rejects it before multiplying. This is the recovery boundary: no allocation has occurred and no partial object exists. A tempting alternative, multiplying first and checking whether the result looks small, is harder to reason about and easy to get wrong when signed types or additional arithmetic enter the expression.

slides.title: A conversion is an operation with its own semantics
keyPoints: Unsigned conversion reduces modulo its range
Narrowing can discard information
Validation should precede a meaning-changing cast
slides.narration: Converting negative one to an unsigned type does not preserve the idea of an error indication. It produces the value congruent to negative one modulo that unsigned range, which is the maximum. Narrowing a larger nonnegative value can similarly discard high information. These are defined conversions in the relevant unsigned cases, but their results may violate the application's meaning. A cast documents a requested conversion, not a proof that it is safe for the domain. When parsing a length into a wide signed result, first reject negatives and out-of-range values. Then convert the validated count into the size type used by the storage interface.
actions: Trace negative one and a too-large positive value through a hypothetical narrow unsigned conversion.

question.prompt: What does a static_cast prove about an untrusted length?
question.answer: Only that the requested conversion is expressed in code. It does not prove the original value is nonnegative, within policy, or preserved by the destination type.

slides.title: Promotions can change where arithmetic happens
keyPoints: Small integer operands often promote to int
The expression type matters before assignment
A narrow final result does not imply narrow intermediate arithmetic
slides.narration: Suppose two small unsigned objects contain two hundred and one hundred. On a common platform their addition is performed after promotion to int, which can represent three hundred. Assigning that result to an eight-bit unsigned object then reduces it to forty-four. That path is different from saying a hardware byte addition necessarily occurred. The final stored value may match an eight-bit modular model, but the source-level reasoning must account for the promoted expression type. This becomes especially important with shifts, complements, and comparisons. Inspect operand types and promotion rules before making claims about overflow or signedness from the destination variable alone.
actions: Separate the expression’s intermediate 300 from the final modeled eight-bit result 44.

question.prompt: Does assigning an expression to a small unsigned object force all intermediate operations into that width?
question.answer: No. Promotions and usual arithmetic conversions determine the expression type before the final assignment conversion.

slides.title: Rearrange a bound without performing the risky product
keyPoints: For nonzero width, compare count with limit/width
Handle zero width explicitly
Return a result only after the proof succeeds
slides.narration: The desired condition is count times width no greater than limit. If both quantities are nonnegative and width is not zero, we can check count no greater than limit divided by width before multiplying. Integer division rounds down, which gives exactly the largest whole count that fits. Zero width needs its own branch because division by zero is invalid, while a zero-byte mathematical product may be permitted by the API. The limit should be representable in the destination size type. After this proof, the product is bounded by that limit and can be computed. Keep the checked result with the decision so later callers do not repeat the unsafe calculation.
actions: Use limit 100 and width 12 to derive the largest permitted count without multiplying candidate values.

slides.title: Representation knowledge does not authorize signed overflow
keyPoints: Bit-pattern models have an explicit width
Source arithmetic follows language rules
Use an unsigned magnitude or a checked branch when needed
slides.narration: At the representation level, inverting an eight-bit pattern and adding one gives two's-complement negation modulo two hundred fifty-six. For the minimum pattern, the result is the same pattern. That is a useful description of a fixed-width model. It is not a valid implementation of every ordinary signed absolute value. The source operation still needs a representable result. A program that needs the magnitude of the most negative integer can choose an appropriate unsigned representation and a carefully defined conversion, or reject that input under a narrower contract. Keep representation exercises distinct from executable signed expressions, especially when translating a diagram into C++ code.

slides.title: Boundary tests should target the operation’s proof
keyPoints: Test zero and the largest accepted request
Test the first rejected request
Test maximum type values without evaluating invalid arithmetic
slides.narration: For a checked size calculation, ordinary values confirm only the easy path. Use zero count and zero width to test their chosen policy. Use the exact largest accepted count and the next count to test the division boundary. Use the type's maximum with a multiplier greater than one to make sure the guard rejects before multiplication. For signed increment, test the maximum directly and confirm the rejected result is returned. Avoid a test that itself overflows while computing its expected answer. Test infrastructure follows the same language rules as production code. A mathematical expectation may need a wider model or a hand-derived bound.

slides.title: Review arithmetic as a chain of justified transitions
keyPoints: Input domain → validated values
Validated values → representable operation
Operation result → permitted resource request
slides.narration: A systems count often crosses several boundaries. Text is parsed into an integer. A signed status is recognized as success or failure. A count and width are combined into bytes. Those bytes are checked against a resource policy and passed to an allocator. A defect at an early boundary can make every later check misleading. Review the chain in order, asking what each conversion and operation preserves. The best helper does more than return a plausible number: it states its input domain, reports rejection separately, and delivers a result whose bounds are already established. This reduces repeated arithmetic assumptions as the program grows.
